records.bodyText:
CHAPELLCROSS: WHAT HAPPENED TO THE WIDER VISION, AND WHERE HAS THE PUBLIC MONEY GONE?
The earlier proposals for Chapelcross described a mixed-use employment, energy and innovation site.
The council’s May 2021 programme update included five themes:
• Green energy and net-zero industry.
• Sustainable agriculture, aquaculture and food.
• Clean mobility and logistics.
• Education, skills and training.
• Digital connectivity and data services.
The 2024 masterplan developed that wider approach through hydrogen, green industry, enterprise and energy campuses. It included flexible premises for smaller businesses, manufacturing and supply-chain activity.
Digital infrastructure was already part of the earlier vision. The question is how a development now dominated by hyperscale data centres delivers the wider economic and community benefits originally envisaged? And isn’t just a sudden jump onto the Data Centre bandwagon and a money grab!
Their ongoing use on this public funding now needs a clear explanation. Not the least because what’s now planned is substantially different from what received public funding.
Publicly available and published records show:
• A May 2021 report confirmed a £134,000 NDA payment to Dumfries and Galloway Council under a five-year £495,000 Chapelcross grant agreement.
• A SOSE freedom-of-information response recorded a grant of up to £150,000 over three years from 2022/23 to support the council’s Chapelcross business-case work.
• The council’s November 2024 report identified £15.3 million of proposed government funding through Borderlands, plus £5.5 million committed by the council, for roads and services to unlock the site.
• The Ferret reported this month that the Borderlands allocation was up to £17.3 million. Both Borderlands and the council told it that funding had not yet been awarded and remained conditional.
Now all these figures concern different dates, purposes and funding stages. And so they cannot simply be added together or described as money handed to CX Tech that’s now due to be handed back etc. 
But since the attendees at the first (and only?) public meeting reported that the CX representative stated “hat money would have to be paid back if the site is not developed” it might seem important that the council, Scottish and UK governments and the public get any relevant written explanations.
Questions that now seem important and need a clear legal answer include:
Which organisation received the money, how much, and when?
Which agreement or agreements now contain the repayment requirements?
What precisely triggers any repayment, and by what deadline?
Does any of this require this particular data centre scheme, does this change of plan now invalidate the original funding plan that was far more community oriented?
Could another suitable development meet the conditions of this hyperscale data centre does not?
Which elements of the earlier mixed-use vision remain, and where will they be delivered?
Does ANY of the original bison remain among thes enemies plans?
I remember seeing the original plans and how it was about regenerating a genuinely brownfield site to get some use for the local community and businesses. Not the current exploitative land and cash grab for the usual suspects. 
Please Google and look for the following documents yourself (perhaps the Green Party for example has the manpower and volunteers to dive deeply into this?):
“CX SSG Mark Fulton CX programme May21”
“Chapelcross Development Framework November 2024”
“Chapelcross council 5 November 2024 15.3 5.5”
“SOSE 127 FOI Chapelcross April 2024”
“Chapelcross Ferret October 2026 public funds”
I think we need to call on the council, all funding bodies and both governments to now examine and publish (any not available) the funding agreements, payments to date and repayment conditions for the site, CX and all stakeholders. 
The community and tax payers should be able to see exactly what has been funded and what obligations follow.

records.bodyText:
The problem we as a species face, is that AI is a fait accompli.
It has been unleashed way too quickly, before we were ready to comprehend it or prepare for its intrusion into every aspect of our [digital] lives. It arrived completely unregulated, released by tech billionaires who (to quote the character Ian Malcolm in Jurassic Park) were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn't stop to think if they should.
It is here now and it is not going away. And exponentially snowballing demand for it means more and more datacentres to power it will be needed. So simply saying "don't use it" is utterly pointless. Like saying mobile phones and their network infrastructure will go away because you don't use one. The masts will still go up, regardless, as too many other people do. It is already everywhere. You're probably using it already without even realising it. Meta (that Facebook, Instagram, Threads etc is built on), now uses AI tools function. So does Amazon, Ebay, PayPal, your bank, the NHS, passport control, even your online supermarket shopping. It's being snapped up everywhere as a method of generating efficiencies.
We currently denounce and lambaste AI in the same way that luddites did against power looms in the 19th century. Power looms did not go away. Neither will AI. That horse has long since bolted.
However that does not mean that development of datacentres should just be allowed unopposed or unregulated. AI itself might be too far gone to restrain, but the datacentres that house it, still have to conform to planning regulations, environmental law etc. Our MPs, MSPs, councillors, community councils, and local planning officers all must be held accountable to public scrutiny, to ensure all environment safeguards and controls are fully adhered to.

records.bodyText:
TIME TO REOPEN THE FLAWED F/V MISTRESS ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION
OCTOBER 18, 2026
https://www.windtaskforce.org/.../time-to-reopen-the...
The Mayday call for the F/V Mistress was made around 1:30 AM on January 1, 2019. The Coast Guard handwritten notes show the Beacon ID ADCD 02005944C01 at 6:44 AM, and then the search ended between 7:02 and 8:39 AM. The MH-60 helicopter spent 37 minutes looking for the ship.
The wind speeds in the area were 35 knots, with 10-foot waves. The MH-60 regularly conducts search-and-rescue operations in sustained winds of 60 knots. The Coast Guard’s all-weather helicopter was unable to assist because of radar clutter and the turbines being too close together.
Green Oceans in August 2026 located the vessel in a "targeted" dive, 92 feet underwater and only 50 feet from the base of Block Island turbine No. 1 .
The GPS coordinates and distress call data, straight out of the Coast Guard's original handwritten accident file, coincide with the turbine. There may be information that past divers working around the turbine had seen the wreck in past years.
Based on the hull orientation, investigators noted that while the boat was taking on water during the storm, it appears to have made an abrupt starboard avoidance maneuver to dodge the turbine. This sharp turn in rough seas likely caused the 52-foot trawler to roll over and sink immediately.
Green Oceans has asked several federal agencies to reopen Coast Guard Search and Rescue case # 1158048 (associated with MISLE Activity 6618087).
Dr. John DiCecco issued a naval study in January 2019, which focused on boat identification #672568. Dr. DiCecco is a prominent Research Engineer at the Naval Undersea Warfare Center (NUWC) Division Newport in Rhode Island. His work from January 2019, titled “F/V Mistress Navy Analysis,” was a post-accident investigation that utilized Navy sonar assets to analyze underwater imagery and determine the location of the sunken fishing vessel, F/V Mistress, near Block Island.
The investigation relied on a sonar search performed using Navy assets to locate the vessel. It analyzed the January 1, 2019, F/V Mistress accident and resolved "discrepancies" between U.S. Coast Guard coordinate reporting and the actual wreckage location relative to local offshore wind turbines.
After the 2019 sinking, BOEM funded a benthic and epifaunal environmental monitoring program at the Block Island Wind Farm, carried out by field researchers from the University of Rhode Island and HDR Engineering. On page 184 of their subsequently published OCS Study (BOEM 2020-044), right above Figure 79, researchers explicitly noted "partial boat debris" on the seafloor during the final day of a biological dive survey later in 2019 near turbine #1
Attached is a file referencing a sonar search performed using Navy assets. It’s unclear how or why the Navy has been so specifically involved.
Importantly, the GPS coordinates used to direct this search are transposed from the USCG reporting.
Time to reopen the investigation

Lies about water
In a reply to my FOI request, Scottish Water produced a copy of their letter to ILI telling them there is not sufficient capacity in the existing system in Fife to supply Cato and that the volume of water is so high it will have to be drawn from a service reservoir in Glendevon. However, ILI made no mention of this whatsoever in their subsequent planning application and in fact they said Scottish Water had simply told them there was "existing capacity". This is both a serious omission and a lie on ILI's part. Their application contains very little information about water quantities and sources, and it is only via FOI requests that the truth is slowly being revealed....

records.bodyText:
This is an interesting piece in The Telegraph - Microsoft has pulled out of the NScale Essex data centre.  Microsoft was its only customer.  
From September last year:
Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said the UK was on its way to becoming a world leader in AI.
"Meaning more jobs and investment, more money in people's pockets, and transformed public services"  BBC
But, in the same article:
AI expert Dr Haider Raza said "awful" electricity costs could also stunt growth.
"We have to make data centres more efficient. This point is very, very important."
We have applications for data centres springing up all over the UK, many from developers who appear to have no experience of data centre build.  Step forward Intelligent Land Investments, about whom we've posted many times before - although it's maybe a bit unfair to single out that one developer, as there are many more.  
Has ILI actually delivered a data centre, or is its experience principally in proposing and promoting developments? On the evidence reviewed so far, we haven't found a completed ILI data centre.  This is the developer who moved swiftly from housing, to small wind farms, to storage and now to data centres; the firm proposing the 'Stoics' - their grandiose umbrella name for three hyperscale data centres named after the three Stoic philosophers - Cato (that one's in Fife), Aurelius (North Lanarkshire), and Rufus (East Ayrshire) - to allegedly form a Green Digital Corridor linking the West, East and Central Scotland.  (We do grudgingly admire their concept, but does that translate into workable data centres?)
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/.../microsoft-axes-ai.../...
'Microsoft has pulled out of an Essex data centre deal in a blow to British company Nscale’s plans for a multibillion-dollar listing.
The US tech giant, one of Nscale’s two largest customers, recently informed the company that it was pulling the plug on its agreement, which was announced last year.
It is a significant setback for Nscale, given Microsoft was to become the anchor tenant at the company’s first British data centre in Loughton, Essex.
Microsoft’s decision threatens to undermine Nscale’s attempts to push ahead with a Wall Street flotation worth up to $35bn (£26bn), despite a brutal sell-off in AI computing stocks.
Rival data centre developers have seen their share prices plunge over the last week on concerns that they will struggle to repay their debts as interest rates and inflation continue to rise.
The outcome of Nscale’s attempted stock market listing will be viewed as a crucial litmus test of investors’ continued appetite for debt-hungry AI businesses. Its success or otherwise will also have implications for Britain’s broader aspirations for the technology.
Nscale, which is backed by tech giants including Nvidia, has positioned itself as Britain’s “sovereign” data centre provider.
Ministers have talked up its Essex data centre project as emblematic of the UK’s AI ambitions, and have lobbied local councillors to push it through.
Microsoft’s backing for the project formed part of £22bn in UK investments promised by the tech company last year during Donald Trump’s state visit. Sir Keir Starmer said it was a step towards Britain “becoming a world leader in AI”.
The data centre site, which contains thousands of high-end Nvidia AI chips, was originally intended to come online next year.
However, it has faced repeated delays, with grid bosses telling Nscale that they do not expect a power supply until the 2030s.
Microsoft’s cancellation leaves the site in apparent limbo. The company was its only announced customer, having agreed to rent 23,000 Nvidia AI chips at the facility. Financing for the data centre boom hinges on securing long-term commitments from AI giants to buy up capacity.
More than 40pc of Nscale’s $103bn in contracted revenue comes from Microsoft, although the UK deal is believed to be a small part of that. Anthropic is another major customer.
Nscale, which boasts heavyweights including former Facebook executives Sheryl Sandberg and Sir Nick Clegg on its board, has been privately valued at $15bn.
It is seeking to raise billions of dollars in a float that could value it at more than twice that, making it one of Britain’s most valuable AI companies.
However, its plans have clashed with a major sell-off in AI infrastructure businesses amid questions about the data centre building boom.
Tech analyst Gartner said last week that $3.5tn could be written off by 2030 if the AI boom fails to deliver on its promises.
Separately, Nscale has also faced delays at a flagship data centre in Norway, reportedly leading to heavy penalties.
Australian rival Firmus cancelled plans for a $20bn IPO earlier this month, citing market conditions. Other “neocloud” companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius have seen their shares and bonds slump.
Neoclouds are heavily dependent on raising new investment and debt to keep building, and soaring market interest rates have increased concerns about the sustainability of their business models.
An Nscale spokesman said: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK.
“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”
Microsoft did not comment.
Nscale was founded by Australian entrepreneur Josh Payne, a former coal miner, just two years ago, and has faced scrutiny for signing large contracts despite a lack of a track record in building data centres.
However, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, praised Nscale on Wednesday at an event in London, saying: “You could be the most valuable UK startup they have created in the last 10 years.”
High electricity prices and long waits for grid connections have been seen as a major barrier to building AI infrastructure in Britain.
In April, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI suspended plans for a “Stargate” AI facility with Nscale on Tyneside, citing Britain’s high electricity prices.'
